title: Questioning First Impressions
keyIdea: When something puzzling happens, split what you saw from your guess about why. Leo bumped my tray is what happened; he did it on purpose is a guess about his intention. A first thought is only one possible reason, so think of at least two others: the queue was crowded, he tripped. Feeling sure is not evidence. Pause, look for clues, and check with a calm question such as Did you mean to? Follow the clues either way: sometimes they show it was an accident, sometimes you cannot tell yet, and sometimes someone really did mean it.

kid: Picture this. Leo bumps your tray and your lunch nearly falls. Your first thought is fast: he did that on purpose! But hold on. What did you actually see? You saw a bump. That is what happened. On purpose is a guess about why, because you cannot see inside Leo's head.

A first thought is just one idea. Try to find two more. Maybe the queue was crowded and someone pushed him. Maybe he tripped on a bag. Now you have three possible reasons, and you do not know yet which one is true.

Feeling very sure does not make a guess right. Clues do. Did he say oops? Was he carrying a lot? Some clues point to an accident. Some leave you unsure. And sometimes the clues show a person really did mean it, like someone who grabs your pen, laughs and will not give it back.

So, when a first thought makes you hot, use four steps. Notice the hot thought. Pause and breathe. Think of two other reasons. Then check: ask a calm question, such as Did you mean to bump me? A question lets the other person explain. Did you do that on purpose?! is blaming, not asking.
adult: This topic is about reading other people's intentions. Psychologists call one habit hostile attribution bias. It means assuming bad intent when a situation is unclear. Kenneth Dodge's research links it to more conflict. It also shows the habit can shrink when children learn to think of other reasons and check them. Therapists call a related thinking trap mind reading: treating a guess about what someone thinks as a fact.

The skills match PSHE and CASEL goals for ages 9 to 11. Children learn to tell what they saw from how they read it. They take another person's view, think of at least two other reasons and weigh the evidence. They also calm the first hot feeling and check their guess politely. Useful words: assumption, intention, evidence, interpretation and perspective.

Common mistakes: treating the first guess as fact; taking a strong feeling as proof; always and never thinking (he always does this) after one event; checking with a loaded question (why did you do that on purpose?) that is really blame; and acting on the guess with revenge or gossip. Do not overcorrect, though. The aim is not to call everything an accident. When the clues show real unkindness, a child should see it and get help.

In the lab your child sorts sentences into what happened and a guess about why. They pick two other reasons for three puzzling moments. They open clue cards and drag a sure-o-meter to accident, can't tell yet or on purpose. Then they put notice, pause, think and check in order and drag calm words onto a story. Every drag has a button twin.

familyTip: Next time your child says someone was mean, ask two questions: what did you actually see, and what else could explain it? Aim for two other reasons before deciding. If the clues still point to unkindness, take it seriously.

visual.caption: What happened, or a guess about why? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Kai did not reply to my message.
Mo stepped on my foot in the corridor.
Nia sat at a different table today.
Nia does not want to be my friend.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: split fact from guess, find other reasons, weigh clues on a sure-o-meter, order pause-think-check and choose words that check, not blame.

practice.prompt: Sam walked past Ella without saying hello. Which sentence is a fact, not a guess?
practice.hint: A fact is something Ella could see or hear. A guess is about what is in Sam's head.
practice.explain: Ella saw that Sam did not say hello. Why he did not is a guess: he may not have seen her.

practice.prompt: Your first thought is one possible reason. Then you think of {a} more reasons. How many possible reasons do you have now?
practice.hint: Count the first thought, then add the new reasons.
practice.explain: 1 first thought + {a} more = {=a+1} possible reasons. The first thought is only one of them.

practice.prompt: Tom feels completely sure that Jas tripped him on purpose. What does that feeling prove?
choices: Nothing yet: a feeling is not a clue
practice.hint: Ask: what did Tom see or hear, apart from his own feeling?
practice.explain: Feeling sure is not evidence. Tom needs clues, or he can ask Jas calmly what happened.

practice.prompt: Imagine that in a crowded corridor, {b} out of every 10 bumps are accidents. Out of 10 bumps, how many are not accidents?
practice.hint: Take the accidents away from the 10 bumps.
practice.explain: 10 − {b} = {=10-b} bumps are not accidents, so most bumps there are accidents. Assuming on purpose would usually be wrong.

pool.prompt: Your friends go quiet when you walk up. Which is another possible reason, not about you?
choices: They had just finished a story
They do not like me any more
pool.hint: Look for a reason that does not assume they were being unkind.
pool.explain: They may simply have finished a story. The other two choices repeat the same unkind guess.

pool.prompt: Which is the best way to check what happened after Leo bumped your tray?
choices: Did you mean to bump me?
Why did you do that on purpose?!
pool.hint: A good check is a real question. It does not decide the answer for him.
pool.explain: Did you mean to? lets Leo explain. On purpose?! is an accusation, and bumping back acts on a guess.

pool.prompt: Mia thinks: Ana always ignores me. Ana did not wave once today. What is wrong with Mia's thought?
choices: One moment does not prove always
Mia should never think about it
pool.hint: Look at the word always. How many times did it happen?
pool.explain: Always and never are signs of a hot thought. One missed wave is not a pattern.

pool.prompt: Jo grabs your pen, laughs, says Mine now! and will not give it back for the third time this week. What fits the clues?
choices: Jo probably meant it, so get help
pool.hint: Questioning first thoughts means following the clues, not always saying accident.
pool.explain: Jo's words and the repeated grabbing are strong clues that it was on purpose. Tell an adult or ask firmly for it back.

pool.prompt: Put these in the right order: Check, Notice the hot thought, Think of other reasons, Pause. Which comes first?
pool.hint: You have to spot the hot thought before you can slow it down.
pool.explain: Notice the hot thought first, then pause, then think of other reasons, then check.

pool.prompt: Maya did not save you a seat. You never told her you wanted one. How sure can you be that she meant to leave you out?
choices: Not sure: I cannot tell yet
Very sure it was an accident
pool.hint: Do the clues point one way, or are they too thin to tell?
pool.explain: Maya may not have known. The clues do not show either way, so ask her before deciding.

pool.prompt: To pause, you take {s} slow breaths. Each breath takes 4 seconds. How many seconds does your pause last?
pool.hint: Multiply the number of breaths by 4 seconds.
pool.explain: {s} breaths × 4 seconds = {=4*s} seconds, long enough for the first hot feeling to settle.

pool.prompt: Rina lists {a} reasons why Kai might be quiet. {b} of them are unkind guesses about her. How many are other reasons?
pool.hint: Take the unkind guesses away from all the reasons.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} other reasons, so there is more than one way to explain why Kai is quiet.

pool.prompt: Which word means what someone meant to do?
pool.hint: It is the hidden part you cannot see: what was in their mind.
pool.explain: Intention is what someone meant to do. Evidence is the clues, and perspective is how things look from where they stand.
